passage:
“So which side are you on, Yamini?” Devika asked in the corridor outside the design studio, two of her teammates behind her.
“Neither. I just want the brand launch to go well.”
“Neutral means you're with them,” Devika said.
An hour later Karan, the creative head, caught Yamini at the printer. “Devika's people have been moving your files. Where will you sit at the offsite?”
“With both teams, I hope.”
Karan shrugged. On Friday, when a delay was pinned on “people who avoid commitment,” neither camp spoke up. Only Farid, the quiet senior designer, said, “Yamini sent her part on Tuesday. I have the email.” Yamini looked at him, surprised.

qa.q: What did Karan say Devika's people had been doing?
qa.a: Karan said Devika's people had been moving Yamini's files.

qa.q: Why did Yamini answer, “Neither. I just want the brand launch to go well”?
qa.a: Yamini wants to stay out of the rival camps and believes the work matters more, though the answer leaves both sides suspicious.

qa.q: What helped Yamini when the delay was blamed on “people who avoid commitment”?
qa.a: A quiet ally, Farid, spoke up with the email showing Yamini had sent her part on time, which protected Yamini when neither camp did.

qa.q: How might Devika have seen Yamini's “Neither”?
qa.a: Devika seems to read it as taking the other side, since Devika said, “Neutral means you're with them.”

grounding: An employee tries to stay out of rival camps, is pressed by both, and is protected only by a quiet ally.

passage: I'm Sachin, and for two years I told myself neutrality was a virtue. Our department had two camps, one loyal to Hemant, the regional head, the other to the operations director. Both kept asking me for news about the other. I gave each the same polite answer: “I only do my job.” It felt principled. Then a shipment went wrong, and each camp assumed I'd told the other side. Hemant stopped copying me on mails. The director's team stopped inviting me to lunch. When the review came, nobody defended me because nobody thought I was theirs. Only Bhavna, from stores, said quietly, “The records are clean. I checked them.” Looking back, I needed a couple of people like that before things went wrong.

qa.q: What polite answer did Sachin give both camps?
qa.a: Sachin said, “I only do my job.”

qa.q: Why did Sachin see neutrality as a virtue?
qa.a: Sachin felt principled and comfortable staying out of both camps, without seeing that neutrality left no one to speak up for Sachin.

qa.q: What might Sachin have done earlier to avoid being squeezed?
qa.a: Sachin could have built a few quiet allies who trust Sachin's work, as Bhavna did, before any crisis, and kept clear records.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been thinking when Bhavna said, “The records are clean. I checked them”?
qa.a: Bhavna probably wanted to be fair and speak from the evidence, though nobody else in the review would.

grounding: An employee tries to stay out of rival camps, is pressed by both and is left unprotected without clear, quiet allies.
